newsitem.title: CUBA: U.S. OK does not mean media can pour into Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OK does not mean media can pour into Cuba.

text.p: Reports on Wednesday that the United States was about to authorise some U.S. media to set up offices in Cuba do not mean all those organisations can come to the island right away, a Cuban government official said.

So far Cuba has granted only Cable News Network (CNN) permission to set up a permanent office in Havana, Frank Gonzalez, director of the Foreign Ministry's International Press Centre (CPI), told Reuters.

This means CNN, which has been waiting for U.S. permission and according to U.S. sources is on the list to be granted approval, now appears to have the green light to become the first U.S. news organisation to have a permanent office on the island since 1969. But the others may have to wait a while.

Gonzalez said he was aware of news reports from Washington that the White House would shortly announce it was granting licenses to a string of U.S. news organisations. CNN was on the list, U.S. sources said in Washington.
"The Cuban government has only authorised CNN," Gonzalez said. "We have various other requests ... the government of Cuba will decide if they open or do not open bureaus."

President Fidel Castro's government announced in November it was granting permission to CNN to set up a bureau. It said the decision was taken because of good relations between Cuba and CNN, whose founder, Ted Turner, met Castro several times.

Gonzalez gave no indication when or whether other U.S. news organisations would be granted permission by Cuba to set up offices on the island. He also did not say which news organisations had requests pending.

One U.S. source said the approval would be granted to the CNN, Univision, CBS and ABC television network; to the Miami Herald, Chicago Tribune and Fort Lauderdale Sun-Sentinel newspapers and to the Associated Press and Dow Jones news agencies. Approval would also be given to the School of Advanced International Studies at the private Johns Hopkins University, the source said.

Although they have been barred from setting up offices, representatives of some U.S. media do visit the island regularly. Like journalists from other countries, they are required to apply for a special visa, which Cuban authorities may or may not grant.

But despite longstanding hostilities between the Cuban and U.S. governments and the 35-year-old U.S. economic embargo, Castro's government appears well aware that a key target audience for Cuba's point of view is the United States.
Castro, who is 70, very rarely gives intervews, but when he has done so in the last few years almost all have been with U.S. news media.

Gonzalez said some 100 foreign journalists from about 30 countries were now permanently accredited in Cuba. These include journalists from news agencies such as Reuters, Agence France Presse and EFE and from newspapers such as El Pais of Spain and the Financial Times of London.
